slides.text: JOHAR. The Chhattisgarhi word of greeting and farewell. Of recognition and respect. Spoken to those you see completely — not just their face but their whole person, their whole history, their whole courage. This series says Johar to Chhattisgarh, to Gandhi, and to everyone who gave everything.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: The word JOHAR in large Devanagari script, golden, against the Chhattisgarh landscape — its forests, rivers, ancient forts. The finale. The greeting that is also a farewell. The recognition that the whole series has been building toward. Warm, complete, luminous.

slides.text: This series began in 1825 with Gaind Singh — the first martyr of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement. It ends in 1933 with Gandhi's departure. One hundred and eight years of resistance. One word that holds all of it: Johar.
slides.visualDescription: The arc of the series: 1825 Gaind Singh to 1933 Gandhi's departure. One hundred and eight years on screen. A timeline that is also a river — flowing from the first act of resistance to the last visit. The series as a single sustained act of Johar to a century of courage.

slides.text: Johar to Gaind Singh — the first martyr of Chhattisgarh, hanged by the British for resisting the colonial salt tax in 1825. He died before Gandhi was born. He died for the same freedom. He is the beginning of this story.
slides.visualDescription: Gaind Singh — 1825, the first martyr. His face, his hanging, his cause: the salt tax resistance that preceded Gandhi's Salt March by 105 years. The series' first episode acknowledging its deepest root. Johar to the man who began what would take a century to complete.

slides.text: Johar to Veer Narayan Singh — who died at Jaistambh Chowk in Raipur in 1857, the first martyr of the 1857 uprising in Chhattisgarh. Who stole grain from a merchant's warehouse to feed starving people and was hanged for it. The Robin Hood of Chhattisgarh's freedom story.
slides.visualDescription: Veer Narayan Singh at Jaistambh Chowk, 1857 — the hanging that the British tried to make an example of and instead made a martyr. The grain taken for starving people. The cannon that fired. The man who became the symbol of principled defiance. Johar.

slides.text: Johar to Gundadhur — the Dhurwa tribal leader of the 1910 Bastar Bhumkal uprising. Who organised the largest tribal uprising in Chhattisgarh's history against forest and land exploitation. Who was never caught by the British. Who disappeared into the forest and into legend.
slides.visualDescription: Gundadhur — the unconquered. Never photographed, never caught, described only by those who saw him. The 1910 Bhumkal uprising. Thousands of tribals. The forest as both cover and cause. His disappearance into legend as the most complete form of victory against documentation.

slides.text: Johar to Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — who organised the Chhattisgarh freedom movement for two decades before Gandhi came, who placed the sacred thread on Harijan men when no one else would, who built the Satnam Ashram, who brought Gandhi to Chhattisgarh. Gandhi's guru.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — two decades of work before Gandhi arrived, the Janeu movement, the Satnam Ashram, the invitation to Calcutta that brought Gandhi to Raipur. Gandhi calling him guru. The architect of the first visit and the man who gave Gandhi something to honour in the second.

slides.text: Johar to Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — who organised the Kandel Satyagraha, who refused a false tax on water, who heard his name from Gandhi's lips before 15,000 people in Dhamtari, who stayed in Dhamtari all his life. The complete Satyagrahi.
slides.visualDescription: Babu Chhotelal Srivastava — in the paddy field at Kandel in 1920, in the crowd at Makai Chowk when Gandhi names him, in Dhamtari for the rest of his life. The man who won the most local of victories and made it the foundation of the most national of movements.

slides.text: Johar to Narayan Rao Meghawale — who co-led the Kandel Satyagraha, who was imprisoned in Raipur Jail with Sharma, who made salt from Dhamtari pond water in 1930 in solidarity with Dandi, who received Gandhi in 1933 still committed, still complete.
slides.visualDescription: Narayan Rao Meghawale — the co-leader of the Kandel movement, the prisoner, the salt-maker. His face across the decade from 1920 to 1933. The continuity of commitment made human. Johar to the man who found multiple forms for the same essential resistance.

slides.text: Johar to Ravi Shankar Shukla — who signed the DCC papers in 1920 as first secretary, who housed Gandhi in 1933, who became the first Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh in 1947. The man whose arc is the arc of the Chhattisgarh freedom movement made personal.
slides.visualDescription: Ravi Shankar Shukla — 1920 DCC secretary, 1933 host of Gandhi, 1947 first CM of Madhya Pradesh. The three moments of one man's complete commitment. The DCC founding papers, Shukla Niwas, Sitabardi Fort 1947. The full arc in three images.

slides.text: Johar to Thakur Pyarelal Singh — who left the practice of law in 1920, who organised the freedom movement in Raipur's district, who paid the price of principle with his professional career and continued anyway. The lawyer who chose the movement over the law.
slides.visualDescription: Thakur Pyarelal Singh — hanging up his barrister's robe in 1920, walking out of his office, not looking back. His face after the decision: at peace. The career gone. The commitment intact. The lawyer who found that the movement was a better brief than any colonial court would offer.

slides.text: Johar to Abbas Bhai — who drove Gandhi to Dhamtari when a police officer said he could not, who lost his Raipur Bus Service license for doing what was right, who did not regret it. The ordinary man who paid the ordinary extraordinary price.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai — at the wheel of his motor on the Raipur-Dhamtari road, facing the police officer, driving on. Then: the canceled license notice. His face: no regret. The transport operator who transported the freedom movement and paid with his transport company.

slides.text: Johar to Omar Seth of Gurur — who lifted Gandhi on his shoulders at Makai Chowk so that 15,000 people could see him. Not famous. Not in any national history. Known only in Dhamtari. The strength of his shoulders: the movement's most essential infrastructure.
slides.visualDescription: Omar Seth of Gurur — lifting Gandhi above the Makai Chowk crowd. The image of strength in service of an idea. No national recognition. Local legend. His shoulders as the infrastructure that made Gandhi visible to 15,000. Johar to the man history forgot to write down.

slides.text: Johar to Dayavati of Tamora — who stood before a British rifle and did not move. Whose village was renamed Gandhigram by Gandhi. Whose name is known in Tamora and nowhere else in the national record. The undefeated woman. The Chhattisgarhi heroine history forgot.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati — the chest forward, the rifle aimed, the not-moving. Her name. Her village. Her erasure from the national record. Her permanence in the local memory. Her face as the most complete portrait of what women gave and what history failed to count.

slides.text: Johar to Amar Singh and his wife — who shouted Gandhi's name while being beaten, who together refused to change their slogan at any cost. His name in the record, hers not. Both of them equally present in the moment. Both deserve this Johar equally.
slides.visualDescription: Amar Singh and his wife — together in the Tamora beating. His name recorded, hers not. The series speaking both their names here: Amar Singh, and his wife whose name we do not have but whose courage we can see. The Johar given equally to both.

slides.text: Johar to Mohammad Yunus — who stood before the magistrate and chose jail over compromise, who gave his seventeen-village zamindari, his hundreds of acres, his cattle, and his gold to the principle of not cooperating with an unjust colonial authority.
slides.visualDescription: Mohammad Yunus — his declaration in the courtroom, his zamindari confiscated, his walk to jail. The total sacrifice: seventeen villages, hundreds of acres, cattle, gold. Everything. In exchange for one thing: the right to say no. Johar to the man who paid everything for the word no.

slides.text: Johar to Makhan the barber — who cut Gandhi's hair at Victoria Garden before one lakh people, who asked to touch Gandhi's feet, who received a rupee and never spent it. The Harijan man who was honoured by the Mahatma and kept the honour in his pocket for life.
slides.visualDescription: Makhan the barber — his hands in Gandhi's hair, his touching of Gandhi's feet, his kept rupee. The man whose dignity was formally acknowledged by the most famous man of his age. The rupee as the monument. The kept coin as the permanent record of a moment of recognition.

slides.text: Johar to the women of Machilabad — who gave their gold rings and silver bangles to the Tilak Fund in December 1920. Muslim women, Hindu women, together. Named in the record only as 'the women of Machilabad.' Their generosity recorded, their names erased. Both the giving and the erasure are true.
slides.visualDescription: The women of Machilabad — their gold and silver in the Tilak Fund bag. Their names absent from the record. The giving permanent, the givers unnamed. The Johar given to the category the record created in place of their names. Acknowledged. Counted. Given the word they were never given.

slides.text: Johar to the 500 from Dhamtari who went to the Nagpur Congress session and voted for Non-Cooperation. 500 ordinary people who traveled to a national session, raised their hands, and cast their vote for the freedom of India. The movement made democratic.
slides.visualDescription: The 500 from Dhamtari at the Nagpur session — their hands raised among thousands. Ordinary farmers, workers, students from the Kandel district. Their votes mattering. The movement democratic in the most literal sense: 500 ordinary people voting for freedom.

slides.text: Johar to Prabhu Lal Kabra — who stood on the Raipur platform in December 1920 as a young man and recorded in his memory what he saw: Gandhi in third class, hands folded, the train still moving. His testimony: the most complete record of the arrival. The eyewitness who held the memory.
slides.visualDescription: Prabhu Lal Kabra — young, on the Raipur platform in 1920, watching. His memory holding what no camera captured: Gandhi in third class, hands folded, train moving. His testimony preserved in writing. The eyewitness as the archive. The human memory as the most reliable record.

slides.text: Johar to E. Raghavendra Rao — who built the Congress organisation in Bilaspur across decades, who received Gandhi in 1933, who is among the least celebrated figures of the Chhattisgarh movement. The builder whose structure outlasted his name.
slides.visualDescription: E. Raghavendra Rao — the invisible organiser, the builder of the Bilaspur Congress. His structure standing after his name faded from memory. The Johar to those who built what others were seen in. The foundation honouring made visible.

slides.text: Johar to the thirty-nine Jungle Satyagrahis of 1922 — who entered the reserved forest deliberately and were arrested. Who received 3 to 5 months imprisonment. Who won minimum wages and the end of forced labour. Thirty-nine people whose names we do not have, whose victory we have.
slides.visualDescription: The thirty-nine Jungle Satyagrahis — entering the forest in their organised line, being arrested, in jail. Their names unknown. Their victory permanent: minimum wages, no forced labour. Thirty-nine unnamed people whose sacrifice purchased a named and permanent right. Johar.

slides.text: Johar to Vamanrao Lakhe — who surrendered his Rai Sahab title the day Non-Cooperation was announced, who was given the title Popular by the people of Raipur. The exchange of allegiances: empire's medal returned, people's love received. The economics of dignity.
slides.visualDescription: Vamanrao Lakhe — the medal on the British desk, the people's garland received. Popular: the title that replaced Rai Sahab. The exchange as a complete political statement. Johar to the man who chose the title the people gave over the title the empire bestowed.

slides.text: Johar to the Kandel farmers — who refused to pay a false water tax in August 1920, who stood in their flooded paddy fields and said no, whose Satyagraha Gandhi honoured by coming to Dhamtari. The farmers whose canal still flows, whose victory still holds, whose names we do not have.
slides.visualDescription: The Kandel farmers of August 1920 — standing in their flooded paddy fields, refusing the false tax. Their names unknown. The canal still flowing. The victory still holding. The farmers who began everything. The Satyagrahis who won before Gandhi arrived. Johar.

slides.text: Johar to the Chhattisgarh that received Gandhi twice. That sent him back to Nagpur with 500 delegates, with the Tilak Fund enriched, with the Harijan Fund filled, with a province changed. The land that gave as much as it received. The land of 36 forts that held.
slides.visualDescription: Chhattisgarh as the recipient and giver of two visits — the land receiving Gandhi and giving him proof, resources, commitment. The land of 36 forts standing unchanged behind the human drama. The forests, rivers, plains: the permanent ground beneath the temporary drama of history.

slides.text: Johar to Gandhi. Not the bronze statue Gandhi, not the currency Gandhi, not the national holiday Gandhi — but the Gandhi who sat in third class, who listened more than he spoke, who went where the need was greatest, who called a Chhattisgarhi reformer his guru.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi — the real Gandhi, not the monument. In the third-class compartment. On the ground with Harijan children. Eating at Devri. Listening to Tamora's stories. Calling Sharma guru. The Gandhi who was most himself when he was most simple. Johar to the real man.

slides.text: Gandhi came to Chhattisgarh twice. The first time: three days in December 1920. The second time: five days in November 1933. Eight days total. This series: twenty episodes, 740 slides, dedicated to those eight days and the century they contained.
slides.visualDescription: Eight days — the arithmetic of Gandhi's Chhattisgarh presence. Against it: twenty episodes, 740 slides, the century of resistance they represent. The mathematics of the series as its own tribute. Eight days made into a world. The measure of what eight days can mean.

slides.text: The book Johar Gandhi, by Amir Hashmi. Two to three years of research. Descendants of the Satyagrahis interviewed. Archives consulted. Living memory recorded before it could be lost. The book as an act of recovery. This series as the book's digital extension.
slides.visualDescription: The book Johar Gandhi — its cover, its pages, the author Amir Hashmi's research visible in its specificity. Two to three years of recovered memory. The descendants interviewed. The archives consulted. The living memory recorded. The book and this series as one continuous act of recovery.

slides.text: This series was made so that the schoolchild who passes Gandhi Chowk knows what happened there. So that the farmer who irrigates beside the Kandel canal knows who stood there in August 1920. So that Dayavati's name is spoken beyond Tamora. So that the eight days are not forgotten.
slides.visualDescription: The series' purpose made explicit: the schoolchild at Gandhi Chowk, the farmer at Kandel canal, the village of Tamora — all of them receiving the knowledge this series carries. The series as the act of transmission. The knowledge finding its way to where it belongs.

slides.text: August 15, 1947. India becomes independent. The Chhattisgarh freedom movement's ultimate purpose achieved. Ravi Shankar Shukla hoists the flag. The 500 who went to Nagpur in 1920 are old now — some gone. But what they voted for: here, in the flag.
slides.visualDescription: August 15, 1947 — the Indian tricolor rising at Sitabardi Fort. Shukla raising it. Around him: the old fighters. Some whose names we know. Most whose names we don't. The flag as the answer to what they voted for in 1920. The Nagpur resolution's final consequence.

slides.text: November 1, 2000. The state of Chhattisgarh is formed. The land of 36 forts named for itself at last. The 1825 martyrdom, the 1857 uprising, the 1920 visits, the 1930 Satyagrahas, the 1947 independence — all of it leading to this: a state with its own name, its own government, its own recognition.
slides.visualDescription: November 1, 2000 — the Chhattisgarh state flag rising. The new state's first moments. Behind it: the 175 years from Gaind Singh to statehood. The complete arc from first martyr to final recognition. The land of 36 forts, at last, named and governed by itself.

slides.text: The Kandel canal still flows. The Kankalipara bricks are in some homes still. The Baithd School still stands. Gandhi Chowk is still navigated. Gandhigram Tamora is still named. The memory continues in matter and name and daily use. The most durable form of history.
slides.visualDescription: The living legacy — the Kandel canal flowing, Gandhi Chowk named, Gandhigram Tamora renamed, the Baithd School standing. The material survival of what happened. The permanence of the small victories. The canal free, the names held, the school open. The memory in matter.

slides.text: The words that close the book Johar Gandhi: 'The words recorded on the pages of history may be blurred, but the words inscribed in the mind, heart, and memory of the people are indelible.' Chhattisgarh gave strength and unconditional support to the freedom movement. Always.
slides.visualDescription: The book's closing words on screen. History's blurred pages. The people's indelible memory. Chhattisgarh's unconditional support. The words as the series' closing argument. The indelible memory as the answer to historical erasure. The mind and heart as the ultimate archive.

slides.text: JOHAR to Gaind Singh. JOHAR to Veer Narayan Singh. JOHAR to Gundadhur. JOHAR to Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. JOHAR to Babu Chhotelal Srivastava. JOHAR to Ravi Shankar Shukla. JOHAR to the 500 of Nagpur. JOHAR to the thirty-nine of the forest. JOHAR to Dayavati.
slides.visualDescription: Each name appearing as the Johar is given — Gaind Singh, Veer Narayan Singh, Gundadhur, Sharma, Srivastava, Shukla, the 500, the thirty-nine, Dayavati. Each name in gold. Each Johar a separate act of recognition. The litany of names as the series' final ceremony.

slides.text: JOHAR to Abbas Bhai. JOHAR to Omar Seth. JOHAR to Mohammad Yunus. JOHAR to Makhan the barber. JOHAR to Amar Singh and his wife. JOHAR to the women of Machilabad. JOHAR to the Chamar women of Devri. JOHAR to the elder who washed Gandhi's feet.
slides.visualDescription: The second litany of Johars — Abbas Bhai, Omar Seth, Mohammad Yunus, Makhan, Amar Singh and wife, the Machilabad women, the Devri women, the foot-washing elder. Each name or category in gold. The Johar given to those who paid the ordinary prices for extraordinary causes.

slides.text: JOHAR to Prabhu Lal Kabra. JOHAR to Narayan Rao Meghawale. JOHAR to Thakur Pyarelal Singh. JOHAR to Vamanrao Lakhe. JOHAR to E. Raghavendra Rao. JOHAR to Ghanshyam Singh Gupta. JOHAR to Badrinath Saw. JOHAR to Bajirao Kridatta.
slides.visualDescription: The third litany — the organisers, the witnesses, the committed. Each name in gold. Kabra, Meghawale, Pyarelal Singh, Lakhe, Rao, Gupta, Saw, Kridatta. The names that history kept and the names it almost lost. All given the same Johar. All equally acknowledged.

slides.text: JOHAR to Gandhi — who came twice, who traveled third class, who listened, who called a Chhattisgarhi reformer his guru, who named Tamora Gandhigram, who ate with Harijan children, who opened doors, who kept faith with the poor in word and body and practice.
slides.visualDescription: The final Johar to Gandhi — all his Chhattisgarh moments in one frame. The third-class compartment. Sharma as guru. Gandhigram Tamora. The Devri meal. The Kurud door opening. The Victoria Garden lakh. Makhan's rupee. The complete Gandhi of the two visits. Johar.

slides.text: JOHAR. The greeting and the farewell. The recognition. The seeing. To everyone who gave everything to a freedom they may not have lived to see — from Gaind Singh in 1825 to the departing train of November 28, 1933. JOHAR GANDHI. This series: complete.
slides.visualDescription: The final image: the word JOHAR GANDHI — large, golden, luminous — against the full landscape of Chhattisgarh. Its forests, rivers, 36 forts, paddy fields, the Kandel canal, Gandhi Chowk. All of it held in two words. The series complete. The greeting and the farewell. JOHAR.
